<reason>Side A (CON) won the decisive mechanical clash: B's "money or hours, not both" trap collapsed once A showed savings come from fifth-day buses/cafeteria/heat (which B had already conceded in B1.4) while hours are preserved by longer days; B's A1 retreated to "I never denied something shrinks; I denied it matters." A also set the counterfactual (an understaffed rural five-day week) and B never described a concrete alternative, ultimately conceding "the honest five-day comparison has a vacancy." A's decision rule tracked the motion cleanly: near-zero learning harm where hours hold cannot outweigh positive savings plus retention. B fought back well with the "ceiling is zero / retention invisible in achievement" reframe and the plausible point that fiscally desperate adopters are the ones likely to compress hours, and B's closing was rhetorically the tightest speech in the debate. But B's harm case rested on predicted compression against A's evidence framing and legal minimums, and B's claim that the four-day district has "the same vacancy" was bare assertion. A's repeated clipping was a real execution cost and its cancellation answer to B's Q2 was somewhat ad hoc, keeping this competitive rather than decisive.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's Rebuttal 1 dismantling of B's "trap": hours are preserved by adding minutes to Tuesday, savings come from Friday's dark building, so the two sit in different budget lines — followed by A's Q1 forcing B to name the shrinking line, which B could only answer by conceding savings exist and arguing they are small.</best_rebuttal>
